title: Where Kambric Began
summary_html: Every print I make starts with someone else's hands.
body_html:
Every print I make starts with someone else's hands. My grandmother Kati painted textiles in her Montreal studio through the late '60s and '70s — bold, saturated, some wild, and some with more child-like whimsy. She never saw most of them made into anything. They sat in the basement of my childhood home for decades after her passing: over 300 original hand-painted designs, just waiting.

I don't remember watching her work. She passed when I was just three. What I do remember is growing up around the results — towels and linens in our house printed with her designs, worn soft and tattered from use. One in particular has stayed with me: a tonal green print of a woman lying in the grass. I loved it.

I was the granddaughter who ended up following in her footsteps artistically, closer than my sisters did. When the archive came to me, it didn't feel like inheritance so much as a job I'd been quietly signed up for without knowing it. I held onto them for over a decade before I even began to seriously consider what to do with them.

Kambric Goods is what I've built around that archive. Every dress, blouse, and print name comes from her paper, not a mood board — though not all the names are hers. Some, like Matyó, come straight from the original designs or their inspiration. Others I've named for the music she would have had on while she painted — the era's soundtrack, folded back into the work.

I trained at FIT, spent my twenties in New York fashion, and eventually landed on the west coast — Fairfax, California now, with my husband and our daughter. But the work is still, at its core, a conversation with someone who isn't here to have it with me anymore. All I can hope is that Kati is proud of the legacy that I am trying to carry forward on her behalf.

This journal is where I'll write about that: the archive, the process, the collections as they come together, and everything in between. Starting here felt right — with her, since nothing at Kambric starts anywhere else.

title: A First Look at SS27
summary_html: Yesterday we spent the day at BayHaus Studios in Sausalito shooting the first images for SS27
body_html:
Yesterday we spent the day at BayHaus Studios in Sausalito shooting the first images for SS27, and it was one of those days that makes a collection feel real.

Ruby was our model, photographed by Melissa McCardle, with makeup by Katie Nash. Having the collection on a person, in a space, and in front of the camera for the first time is always a little bit of a milestone — suddenly all the pieces, fabrics, colors, and ideas that have been living in my head start to have a life of their own.

SS27 brings together two new prints alongside a custom woven jacquard satin developed from a third pattern. The jacquard is fully tonal and intentionally understated, letting the texture and weave create the interest rather than adding another color or print.

The palette is earthy and warm: mustardy gold, espresso, clay, ivory, and sage. There's something familiar about these colors, but together they feel fresh for the collection.

I'm sharing just a small glimpse from yesterday for now — enough to give you a sense of where we're headed, without giving too much away. There's still plenty more to come.

title: A new print, a new dress for Fall
body_html:
Tomorrow we open preorders on the Arielle dress — our newest style, and the debut of a print we've never shown before: Parlor Rose.

Parlor Rose comes from the archive, one of my grandmother Kati's hand-painted designs from her Montreal studio. It's been sitting in the collection for decades, waiting for the right dress. Arielle is it.

Like the Jessie dress before her, the Arielle is named for a dear childhood friend.

The dress is 100% silk. Two colorways: Olive and Terracotta.

Both sit in that in-between season — not quite summer, not quite fall. Here in California, that stretch runs long. We're still in short sleeves through October, so Olive and Terracotta are built to work now and keep working as the weather turns. Olive leans toward the greens and golds of early fall. Terracotta keeps a foot in summer, warmer and more sun-worn.

Preorder opens tomorrow. Limited run, made to order.

title: Chainstitch
summary_html: My fascination with chainstitch embroidery started almost a decade ago, back when I was living and working in Brooklyn.
body_html:
My fascination with chainstitch embroidery started well over a decade ago, back when I was still living in Brooklyn.

I had always loved Western wear, particularly the elaborately embroidered suits made by Nudie Cohn. Like my grandmother, Nudie was an immigrant from Eastern Europe, though his path eventually took him into the world of country music, dressing everyone from Dolly Parton and Porter Wagoner to Elvis Presley. Hello, gold lamé suit.

My first company out of design school was Daisy & Elizabeth, started with my good friend, yes, Elizabeth. We designed and made lingerie in New York City, with a strong Americana and Western influence. That fascination eventually came full circle when we created a capsule collection in collaboration with Nudie's Rodeo Tailors.

That was also when I really fell in love with chainstitch itself. The stitched line has movement and character to it; it feels almost drawn onto the fabric. I think that is part of why it has stayed with me. So much of my work begins with drawing and painting, and chainstitch feels like another way of translating a line by hand. So I learned the craft, and when I moved to California about 8+ years ago, I bought my own vintage chainstitch machine and started taking commissions from my home studio.

Almost ten years later, I still offer custom chainstitch embroidery on scarves and garments through Kambric, and take on individual commissions from my studio in Marin.

The setting has changed since those Brooklyn days, but the attraction hasn't. I still love the craftsmanship, the slight imperfection, and the way a simple line of thread can make something feel more personal and more alive.

title: Gearing Up for FIG Dallas
summary_html: Gearing Up for FIG Dallas — from the Kambric Goods Journal.
body_html:
October 20–22 is coming up fast, and this one feels different — FIG Dallas will be Kambric Goods' first wholesale show, which means the last few weeks have been a mix of excitement and a very long to-do list.

Behind the scenes, we've been building out our wholesale presence on JOOR — Resort 2027, our Studio Collection, and SS27 are all live and ready for buyers to browse. There's something surreal about seeing three seasons of work organized into line sheets, knowing they're about to be in front of people who might carry Kambric into their own shops.

Outside of the collection itself, the piece I'm most excited about is the lookbook we're bringing with us. I wanted it to feel less like a sales tool and more like an art object — something with weight to it. So we're working on a chainstitch-embroidered canvas cover, stretched over board, the kind of thing that could sit on a coffee table. It's been a fun excuse to lean into the embroidery work that's become such a core part of what we do.

There's still packing lists, outreach follow-ups, and a hundred small details between now and Dallas — but it's the good kind of busy. More updates as the show gets closer.
